title: Partial-Order Reduction for Schedule-Abstraction-based Response-Time Analyses of Non-Preemptive Tasks

extraction.paper_name: Partial-Order Reduction for Schedule-Abstraction-based Response-Time Analyses of Non-Preemptive Tasks
extraction.paper_description: This paper introduces Partial-Order Reduction (POR) rules to improve the scalability of Schedule-Abstraction Graph (SAG) based Response-Time Analyses (RTA) for non-preemptive tasks on uniprocessor platforms. The goal is to reduce state-space explosion caused by timing uncertainties, while maintaining exact schedulability analysis and providing safe (but not necessarily tight) worst-case response time (WCRT) bounds.

formal_description.statement: J_i = ([r_min_i, r_max_i], [C_min_i, C_max_i], d_i, p_i) is a job, where C_i IN [C_min_i, C_max_i].

variables.r_min_i: Earliest release time of job i
variables.r_max_i: Latest release time of job i
variables.C_min_i: Best-case execution time (BCET) of job i
variables.C_max_i: Worst-case execution time (WCET) of job i
variables.p_i: Priority of job i (smaller value indicates higher priority)
variables.C_i: Actual execution time of job i

assumptions: Job timing parameters are integer multiples of the system clock.
Jobs are non-preemptive.
Priority ties are broken arbitrarily but consistently.
formal_description.conclusion: This defines the parameters and characteristics of a non-preemptive job J_i.

informal_sketch.intuition: Each job in the system has a set of properties that define its behavior and requirements. These properties include its possible release times, possible execution times, its deadline, and its priority.
steps: A job `J_i` is characterized by an interval for its release time `[r_min_i, r_max_i]`, meaning it can be released at any time within this range.
Its execution time `C_i` is also an interval `[C_min_i, C_max_i]`, indicating the actual execution time can vary.
Each job has a fixed absolute deadline `d_i` by which it must complete.
A priority `p_i` is assigned to each job, determining its scheduling order relative to other jobs (lower value means higher priority).
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
class Job:
    def __init__(self, job_id, r_min, r_max, C_min, C_max, d, p):
        self.id = job_id
        self.r_min = r_min
        self.r_max = r_max
        self.C_min = C_min
        self.C_max = C_max
        self.d = d
        self.p = p
        self.C = None  # Actual execution time, chosen within [C_min, C_max]
        self.r = None  # Actual release time, chosen within [r_min, r_max]
key_insights: Jobs have non-deterministic release and execution times, which introduces uncertainty.
Deadlines are absolute and not affected by release jitter.
Non-preemptive nature means a job, once started, runs to completion without interruption.

formal_description.statement: An execution scenario gamma = (C, R) for a set of jobs J = {J_1, J_2, ..., J_m} is a sequence of execution times C = C_1, C_2, ..., C_m and release times R = r_1, r_2, ..., r_m such that, FORALL J_i IN J, C_i IN [C_min_i, C_max_i] AND r_i IN [r_min_i, r_max_i].

variables.C: Sequence of actual execution times for all jobs in J
variables.R: Sequence of actual release times for all jobs in J
variables.J: The finite set of jobs being scheduled
variables.J_i: An individual job in the set J
variables.C_i: Actual execution time of job J_i in this scenario
variables.r_i: Actual release time of job J_i in this scenario
variables.C_min_i: Best-case execution time of job J_i
variables.C_max_i: Worst-case execution time of job J_i
variables.r_min_i: Earliest release time of job J_i
variables.r_max_i: Latest release time of job J_i

formal_description.conclusion: This defines a specific instance of job parameters (actual release and execution times) within their allowed uncertainty ranges.

informal_sketch.intuition: Since job release and execution times are uncertain, an 'execution scenario' is one specific realization of these uncertainties. It's like picking one exact release time and one exact execution time for every job, within their specified ranges.
steps: For each job `J_i` in the system's job set `J`:
Select a precise execution time `C_i` such that `C_min_i <= C_i <= C_max_i`.
Select a precise release time `r_i` such that `r_min_i <= r_i <= r_max_i`.
Combine all these selected `C_i` values into a sequence `C` and all `r_i` values into a sequence `R`.
The pair `(C, R)` then represents a single, fully determined execution scenario.
key_insights: An execution scenario removes all non-determinism from job parameters.
The system's behavior (schedule) is deterministic for a given execution scenario.
Schedulability analysis must consider all possible execution scenarios.

formal_description.statement: A set of jobs J is schedulable under a given scheduling policy A if there exists no execution scenario of J that results in a deadline miss when scheduled by A.

variables.deadline_miss(J, A, gamma): A boolean function indicating if any job in J misses its deadline under policy A in scenario gamma

formal_description.conclusion: This defines what it means for a job set to be schedulable.

informal_sketch.intuition: A system is considered 'schedulable' if, no matter how the uncertain job parameters (release times, execution times) turn out, all jobs will always complete before their deadlines when managed by the specified scheduler.
steps: Enumerate or consider all possible 'execution scenarios' for the given job set `J`.
For each scenario, simulate the scheduling policy `A` to determine the finish time of every job.
Check if any job's finish time exceeds its deadline in that scenario.
If even one scenario leads to a deadline miss, the job set `J` is deemed unschedulable.
If no scenario results in a deadline miss, then `J` is schedulable.
key_insights: Schedulability is a property of the entire system (job set + policy) under all possible uncertainties.
It's a 'worst-case' guarantee: if it's schedulable, it's always safe.

formal_description.statement: An analysis is an exact schedulability analysis iff (i) for all job sets that are deemed schedulable by the analysis, there is no execution scenario that may result in a deadline miss, and (ii) for all job sets deemed unschedulable by the analysis, there is at least one execution scenario that results in a deadline miss.

variables.Analysis.deems_schedulable(J_set): The analysis concludes J_set is schedulable
variables.Analysis.deems_unschedulable(J_set): The analysis concludes J_set is unschedulable
variables.deadline_miss(J_set, Analysis.policy, ga: A deadline miss occurs for J_set under Analysis's policy in scenario gamma

formal_description.conclusion: This defines the criteria for an analysis to be considered 'exact' in determining schedulability.

informal_sketch.intuition: An 'exact' schedulability analysis is one that is perfectly accurate: it never gives a false positive (says schedulable when it's not) and never gives a false negative (says unschedulable when it actually is).
steps: **Condition (i) - Soundness:** If the analysis declares a job set `J_set` as schedulable, then it must be truly schedulable according to Definition 1 (i.e., no actual scenario leads to a deadline miss).

**Condition (ii) - Completeness:** If the analysis declares a job set `J_set` as unschedulable, then it must be truly unschedulable (i.e., there must exist at least one actual scenario that leads to a deadline miss).
key_insights: Exactness implies both soundness (no false positives) and completeness (no false negatives).
This is the highest standard for a schedulability test.

formal_description.statement: An analysis is an exact response-time analysis (namely, produces tight response-time bounds) iff (i) there is no execution scenario such that any job has a response-time smaller than the best-case response time (BCRT) or larger than the WCRT returned by the analysis for that job, and (ii) for each job, there must be an execution scenario where the job experiences a response time equal to the computed BCRT and another where it experiences the computed WCRT.

variables.response_time(J_i, gamma): The actual response time of J_i in scenario gamma (f_i - r_min_i)
variables.Analysis.BCRT(J_i): The best-case response time computed by the analysis for J_i
variables.Analysis.WCRT(J_i): The worst-case response time computed by the analysis for J_i

formal_description.conclusion: This defines the criteria for an analysis to be considered 'exact' in determining response-time bounds.

informal_sketch.intuition: An 'exact' response-time analysis provides the absolute minimum (BCRT) and maximum (WCRT) possible response times for each job. These bounds are not only safe (never violated) but also achievable (there's a scenario where the job actually experiences that exact min/max response time).
steps: **Condition (i) - Safety of Bounds:** For any job `J_i` and any execution scenario `gamma`, the actual response time `response_time(J_i, gamma)` must always fall within or be equal to the computed bounds: `Analysis.BCRT(J_i) <= response_time(J_i, gamma) <= Analysis.WCRT(J_i)`.

**Condition (ii) - Tightness of Bounds:** For each job `J_i`, there must exist at least one specific scenario `gamma_BCRT` where `J_i` achieves exactly `Analysis.BCRT(J_i)`, and at least one specific scenario `gamma_WCRT` where `J_i` achieves exactly `Analysis.WCRT(J_i)`.
key_insights: Exact response-time analysis provides the true minimum and maximum response times.
It's stronger than just 'safe' bounds, as it guarantees achievability.

formal_description.statement: A POR of a set of jobs J_S is safe iff it maintains both conditions of Definition 3 (i.e., provide an exact schedulability analysis) and satisfies condition (i) in Definition 4 (i.e., derives safe bounds on the response time).

variables.J_S: A set of jobs considered for reduction
variables.condition_i_of_Definition_4(POR_method): POR_method satisfies condition (i) of Definition 4 (safety of response-time bounds)

formal_description.conclusion: This defines what constitutes a 'safe' Partial-Order Reduction.

informal_sketch.intuition: A 'safe' Partial-Order Reduction (POR) is a technique that simplifies the analysis by grouping job orderings, but without compromising the core schedulability guarantee. It must still correctly identify if a system is schedulable or not, and its calculated response time bounds must always be valid (even if not perfectly tight).
steps: A POR method is safe if it meets two main criteria:
**1. Exact Schedulability:** It must be an 'exact schedulability analysis' (as per Definition 3). This means it correctly identifies all schedulable systems and all unschedulable systems.

**2. Safe Response-Time Bounds:** Its calculated Best-Case Response Time (BCRT) and Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT) for any job must always be valid bounds (as per condition (i) of Definition 4). That is, the actual response time of a job in any scenario must never be less than the computed BCRT or greater than the computed WCRT. (Note: it does not require the bounds to be 'tight' or achievable, only safe).
key_insights: Safety prioritizes correctness of schedulability over tightness of response-time bounds.
It allows for some over-estimation of WCRT or under-estimation of BCRT, as long as the schedulability verdict is correct.

formal_description.statement: Let J_P be the set of jobs already dispatched until reaching state v_p. A job J_j IN J \ J_P is a direct successor for path P ending in vertex v_p iff there exists an execution scenario in which job J_j is dispatched after state v_p and before any other job.

variables.J_j: Candidate job to be dispatched next
variables.P: Path in the SAG ending at v_p
variables.is_dispatched_after(v_p, gamma): J_j is dispatched after the state v_p is reached in scenario gamma
variables.is_dispatched_after(J_j, gamma): J_k is dispatched after J_j in scenario gamma

formal_description.conclusion: This defines a 'direct successor' job in the context of SAG construction.

informal_sketch.intuition: In the Schedule-Abstraction Graph (SAG), a 'direct successor' job from a given state `v_p` is any job that *could possibly* be the very next job dispatched by the scheduler, given some specific execution scenario.
steps: Start from a system state `v_p` where a set of jobs `J_P` have already completed.
Consider any job `J_j` that has not yet been dispatched (`J_j` is in `J \ J_P`).

If there's at least one specific execution scenario (`gamma`) where `J_j` is the *first* job to be dispatched immediately after `v_p` (before any other job not in `J_P`), then `J_j` is a direct successor.
key_insights: Direct successors represent the immediate branching possibilities in the SAG.
It considers all possible execution scenarios to find what *could* be dispatched next.

formal_description.statement: Given a system state v_p, a set of jobs is a safe reduction set (denoted by J_M(v_p)) iff there is no other job in J \ (J_M(v_p) UNION J_P) that can start executing before all jobs in J_M(v_p) finish their execution.

variables.J_M_v_p: A candidate set of jobs for reduction
variables.J_P: Set of jobs already dispatched until v_p
variables.J_x: Any job not in J_M_v_p or J_P
variables.can_start_executing_before_all_finish(J_: J_x can start before all jobs in J_M_v_p complete, starting from v_p

formal_description.conclusion: This defines a 'safe reduction set' for Partial-Order Reduction.

informal_sketch.intuition: A 'safe reduction set' `J_M` is a group of jobs that can be processed together (as a 'batch') because no other job outside this group can 'interfere' by starting its execution before all jobs in `J_M` have finished. This means `J_M` can be treated as an isolated block of work.
steps: Identify a candidate set of jobs `J_M` that are not yet dispatched and are considered for reduction.
Consider all other jobs `J_x` that are neither in `J_M` nor already dispatched (`J_P`).
If, under any possible execution scenario, none of these `J_x` jobs can start executing before *all* jobs in `J_M` have completed, then `J_M` is a safe reduction set.
Essentially, `J_M` forms a 'busy period' that cannot be interrupted by external jobs.
key_insights: The core idea is isolation: jobs in `J_M` do not affect (and are not affected by) jobs outside `J_M` during their execution.
This property allows for abstracting away the internal ordering of jobs within `J_M`.

formal_description.statement: A job J_x IN J \ (J_S UNION J_P) is an interfering job for J_S iff J_x can execute before any of the jobs in J_S.

variables.J_x: A candidate job to check for interference
variables.J_S: A candidate reduction set of jobs
variables.can_execute_before(J_i): J_x can start executing before job J_i (from J_S) starts

formal_description.conclusion: This defines what an 'interfering job' is for a candidate reduction set.

informal_sketch.intuition: An 'interfering job' is any job outside a candidate reduction set `J_S` that could potentially disrupt the execution of jobs within `J_S` by starting before one of them. If such a job exists, `J_S` cannot be a safe reduction set.
steps: Consider a candidate reduction set `J_S` and a job `J_x` that is not in `J_S` and not yet dispatched (`J_P`).
If there's any scenario where `J_x` starts executing before *any* job `J_i` from `J_S` starts, then `J_x` is an interfering job.
This interference can happen due to `J_x` having higher priority or `J_x` being released during an idle period when `J_S` jobs are not yet ready.
key_insights: Interference prevents a set of jobs from being treated as a single, uninterrupted block.
The conditions for interference are critical for determining safe reduction sets.

formal_description.statement: C(t, v_p) = {J_j IN J_S | r_max_j < t}

variables.C_t_v_p: The set of jobs in J_S that are certainly released before time t
variables.J_S: The candidate reduction set of jobs
variables.r_max_j: The latest release time of job J_j

formal_description.conclusion: This defines the set of jobs from a candidate reduction set J_S that are guaranteed to be released by a specific time t.

informal_sketch.intuition: This formula helps identify which jobs from a candidate set `J_S` are definitely available by a certain time `t`. If a job's latest possible release time (`r_max_j`) is before `t`, then it *must* have been released by `t`.
steps: Given a time `t` and a candidate reduction set `J_S`:
Iterate through each job `J_j` in `J_S`.
If `J_j`'s latest release time `r_max_j` is strictly less than `t`, then `J_j` is added to the set `C(t, v_p)`.
key_insights: This set is crucial for reasoning about idle intervals, as a work-conserving scheduler won't be idle if there's a ready job.
It uses `r_max_j` to guarantee release, accounting for release jitter.

variables.J_X: The set of jobs for which to compute the earliest finish time
variables.v_p: The system state from which scheduling begins
variables.A_min_1: The earliest time the processor becomes available after state v_p
variables.J_k: The current job being processed in the loop
variables.J_k.r_min: The earliest release time of job J_k
variables.J_k.C_min: The best-case execution time of job J_k

assumptions: Jobs in J_X are scheduled non-preemptively.
No other jobs (outside J_X) interfere with the execution of jobs in J_X.
formal_description.conclusion: This algorithm computes a lower bound on the earliest time by which all jobs in J_X can complete their execution.

informal_sketch.intuition: To find the absolute earliest time a group of jobs can finish, we assume the best-case scenario: all jobs release as early as possible, execute for their minimum time, and are scheduled in an optimal order (earliest release, then highest priority).
steps: **1. Order Jobs:** Sort the jobs in `J_X` primarily by their earliest release time (`r_min`) in ascending order. If `r_min` values are tied, sort by highest priority (`p`). This ensures we consider jobs that become ready earliest first.
**2. Initialize Finish Time:** Start with `EF_T_val` as the earliest time the processor is available (`A_min_1`) from the previous state `v_p`.
**3. Iterate and Accumulate:** For each job `J_k` in the sorted list:
a. The job `J_k` cannot start before it's released (`J_k.r_min`) and the processor is available (`EF_T_val`). So, its earliest start time is `max(EF_T_val, J_k.r_min)`.
b. Add its best-case execution time (`J_k.C_min`) to this start time to get its earliest finish time. This becomes the new `EF_T_val` for the next job.
**4. Return:** The final `EF_T_val` is the earliest finish time for all jobs in `J_X`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def compute_EFT(job_set_J_X, system_state_v_p):
    # 1. Sort jobs
    sorted_J_X = sorted(job_set_J_X, key=lambda job: (job.r_min, job.p)) # Assuming lower p is higher priority

    # 2. Initialize EF_T_val
    EF_T_val = system_state_v_p.A_min_1 # Earliest processor available time from v_p

    # 3. Iterate and accumulate
    for J_k in sorted_J_X:
        earliest_start_time = max(EF_T_val, J_k.r_min)
        EF_T_val = earliest_start_time + J_k.C_min

    # 4. Return
    return EF_T_val
key_insights: This algorithm simulates a 'greedy' best-case schedule.
Sorting by `r_min` and `p` ensures that jobs are considered in an order that minimizes idle time and maximizes early completion.
Using `C_min` ensures the earliest possible completion for each job.

formal_description.statement: The set of jobs J_X scheduled after state v_p cannot complete its execution earlier than EF_T(J_X, v_p) as returned at line 5 of Algorithm 2.

variables.gamma: Any execution scenario for jobs in J_X
variables.finish_time(J_X, gamma): The actual finish time of all jobs in J_X in scenario gamma
variables.EF_T_J_X_v_p: The earliest finish time computed by Algorithm 2

assumptions: No job J_j IN J \ (J_P UNION J_X) executes between the jobs in J_X (i.e., J_X is an isolated set of jobs).
formal_description.conclusion: EF_T(J_X, v_p) is a valid lower bound on the finish time of J_X.

informal_sketch.intuition: Algorithm 2 calculates the earliest possible finish time by assuming every job releases as early as possible and executes for its minimum duration. Since these are the most optimistic assumptions, no real scenario can possibly result in an earlier completion time.
steps: Algorithm 2 sorts jobs by earliest release and highest priority, then sequentially adds their minimum execution times, respecting release times and processor availability.
This process inherently finds the minimum possible cumulative execution time and minimum possible idle time for the given set of jobs.
Any actual execution scenario will involve release times `r_i >= r_min_i` and execution times `C_i >= C_min_i`.
Therefore, the total workload and potential idle times in any real scenario will be greater than or equal to what Algorithm 2 calculates, meaning the actual finish time cannot be earlier.
key_insights: The proof relies on the fact that `r_min` and `C_min` represent the absolute minimums.
The sequential accumulation in Algorithm 2 ensures that processor availability and release times are always respected, leading to a valid lower bound.

formal_description.statement: The EFT of a safe reduction set J_M is exact iff the set of jobs J_M cannot complete its execution earlier than EFT and there exists an execution scenario such that all jobs in J_M have completed exactly at EFT.

variables.EFT_val: A candidate value for the earliest finish time
variables.J_M: A safe reduction set of jobs
variables.finish_time(J_M, gamma): The actual finish time of all jobs in J_M in scenario gamma

formal_description.conclusion: This defines what an 'exact earliest finish time' means for a safe reduction set.

informal_sketch.intuition: An 'exact' earliest finish time (EFT) is not just a lower bound, but the *tightest* possible lower bound. It means no scenario can finish earlier, and there's at least one specific scenario where the jobs finish at exactly that time.
steps: An `EFT_val` is exact for a safe reduction set `J_M` if two conditions are met:
**1. Lower Bound:** In *all* possible execution scenarios, the actual finish time of `J_M` must be greater than or equal to `EFT_val`.
**2. Achievability:** There must exist at least one specific execution scenario where the jobs in `J_M` complete their execution at precisely `EFT_val`.
key_insights: Exactness combines the concepts of safety (lower bound) and tightness (achievability).
This is a stronger property than just being a 'lower bound'.

formal_description.statement: There exists an execution scenario such that all jobs J_M have completed exactly at EF_T(J_M, v_p) as returned by line 5 of Algorithm 2.

variables.J_M: A safe reduction set of jobs
variables.EF_T_J_M_v_p: The earliest finish time computed by Algorithm 2

assumptions: Each job J_i IN J_M releases at its earliest possible time (r_min_i).
Each job J_i IN J_M executes for its best-case execution time (C_min_i).
The processor becomes available at its earliest possible time (A_min_1) after state v_p.
formal_description.conclusion: The EF_T(J_M, v_p) value computed by Algorithm 2 is achievable in at least one scenario.

informal_sketch.intuition: Algorithm 2 is designed to find the earliest finish time by making the most optimistic assumptions. If we actually create an execution scenario that matches these optimistic assumptions, then the jobs will indeed finish at the time calculated by Algorithm 2.
steps: Construct a specific execution scenario `gamma_exact` where:
a. For every job `J_i` in `J_M`, its actual release time `r_i` is set to `J_i.r_min`.
b. For every job `J_i` in `J_M`, its actual execution time `C_i` is set to `J_i.C_min`.
c. The processor becomes available at `A_min_1` (the earliest possible time from `v_p`).
When Algorithm 2 simulates this `gamma_exact` scenario, it will produce `EF_T(J_M, v_p)` as the finish time.
Therefore, such a scenario exists where `J_M` completes exactly at `EF_T(J_M, v_p)`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def demonstrate_EFT_achievability(job_set_J_M, system_state_v_p, computed_EFT):
    # Create the specific scenario
    gamma_exact = ExecutionScenario(job_set_J_M)
    for J_i in job_set_J_M:
        gamma_exact.release_times[J_i.id] = J_i.r_min
        gamma_exact.execution_times[J_i.id] = J_i.C_min

    # Simulate this scenario
    actual_finish_time = simulate_actual_finish_time(job_set_J_M, gamma_exact, system_state_v_p)

    return actual_finish_time == computed_EFT
key_insights: The algorithm's calculation directly corresponds to a concrete, optimistic execution scenario.
This lemma is crucial for proving the 'tightness' aspect of the exact EFT.

formal_description.statement: The EF_T(J_M, v_p) as returned by line 5 of Algorithm 2 is the exact earliest finish time of J_M.

variables.EF_T_J_M_v_p: The earliest finish time computed by Algorithm 2 for J_M after state v_p
variables.J_M: A safe reduction set of jobs
variables.exact_EFT(J_M): The true exact earliest finish time of J_M as per Definition 8

formal_description.conclusion: Algorithm 2 correctly computes the exact earliest finish time for a safe reduction set.

informal_sketch.intuition: Since we've proven that Algorithm 2's result is both a lower bound (Lemma 6) and achievable (Lemma 7), it must be the *exact* earliest finish time according to our definition of exact EFT (Definition 8).
steps: Recall Definition 8: an EFT is exact if it's a lower bound and it's achievable.
Lemma 6 establishes that `EF_T(J_M, v_p)` (from Algorithm 2) is indeed a lower bound on the finish time of `J_M`.
Lemma 7 establishes that `EF_T(J_M, v_p)` is achievable; there exists a scenario where `J_M` finishes at exactly that time.
Combining these two, `EF_T(J_M, v_p)` satisfies both conditions of Definition 8, thus it is the exact earliest finish time.
key_insights: This corollary formally validates Algorithm 2's output for safe reduction sets.
It's a direct consequence of the preceding lemmas and definition.

formal_description.statement: J_delta = {J_i | J_i IN J_S AND EF_T(C(r_max_i, v_p), v_p) < r_max_i}

variables.J_delta: The set of jobs in J_S before which an idle interval may exist
variables.J_S: The candidate reduction set of jobs
variables.EF_T_C_r_max_i_v_p_v_p: The earliest finish time of jobs in C(r_max_i, v_p) (from Algorithm 2)
variables.C_r_max_i_v_p: The set of jobs in J_S certainly released before r_max_i (from Formula (1))
variables.r_max_i: The latest release time of job J_i

formal_description.conclusion: This defines the set of jobs within J_S that could potentially be preceded by an idle interval.

informal_sketch.intuition: This formula identifies jobs in `J_S` where there might be a gap (idle interval) just before they start. This happens if all jobs that are *certainly* released before `J_i` can finish earlier than `J_i`'s latest release time, leaving the processor idle.
steps: For each job `J_i` in the candidate reduction set `J_S`:
a. Determine the set `C(r_max_i, v_p)`: all jobs in `J_S` that are guaranteed to be released before `J_i`'s latest release time `r_max_i`.
b. Calculate the earliest finish time (`EF_T`) for this set `C(r_max_i, v_p)` using Algorithm 2.
c. If this `EF_T` is strictly less than `J_i.r_max`, it means the processor could potentially be idle after `C(r_max_i, v_p)` finishes, but before `J_i` is certainly released.
d. If this condition holds, `J_i` is added to `J_delta`.
key_insights: This set helps identify potential idle times within the execution of `J_S`.
It uses `r_max_i` to ensure that `J_i` is certainly released, and `EF_T` to check if prior work can finish early.

formal_description.statement: The latest idle interval before the execution of J_i IN J_S cannot end later than r_max_i.

variables.J_S: The candidate reduction set of jobs
variables.idle_interval: An idle interval before J_i starts execution
variables.end_time(idle_interval): The end time of the idle interval
variables.r_max_i: The latest release time of job J_i

assumptions: The scheduling policy is work-conserving.
formal_description.conclusion: This provides an upper bound on the end time of any idle interval immediately preceding a job J_i.

informal_sketch.intuition: A work-conserving scheduler never leaves the processor idle if there's a job ready to run. Since `r_max_i` is the latest time `J_i` can be released, `J_i` is *guaranteed* to be ready at or before `r_max_i`. Therefore, the processor cannot be idle *after* `r_max_i` if `J_i` hasn't started yet.
steps: Assume, for contradiction, that an idle interval before `J_i` ends at `r_max_i + 1` (or any time later than `r_max_i`).
By definition of `r_max_i`, job `J_i` is certainly released by time `r_max_i`.
If the processor is idle at `r_max_i + 1`, it means `J_i` (which is ready) is not being scheduled.
This contradicts the definition of a work-conserving scheduling policy, which states the processor is never idle if a job is ready.
Therefore, the idle interval must end no later than `r_max_i`.
key_insights: The work-conserving property is fundamental here.
`r_max_i` acts as a 'certainty point' for job release, which limits idle periods.

The earliest they could all finish is given by `EF_T(C(r_max_i, v_p), v_p)`, so the idle period cannot start before that.
steps: Consider `J_i` in `J_S` that is released at `r_max_i`.

If an idle interval exists just before `J_i` starts, it implies that all jobs in `C(r_max_i, v_p)` (jobs certainly released before `r_max_i`) must have completed their execution by `r_max_i` (due to the work-conserving property).
We know from Lemma 6 that `EF_T(C(r_max_i, v_p), v_p)` is the earliest possible time these jobs could finish.
Therefore, the idle interval cannot possibly start before `EF_T(C(r_max_i, v_p), v_p)`.

informal_sketch.intuition: If `J_delta` is empty, it means for every job `J_i` in `J_S`, all jobs that are certainly released before `J_i` cannot finish earlier than `J_i`'s latest release time. This implies there's always work to do, preventing idle gaps within `J_S`.
steps: The condition `J_delta = EMPTY_SET` means that for every job `J_i` in `J_S`, `EF_T(C(r_max_i, v_p), v_p) >= r_max_i`.
This implies that the earliest time all jobs certainly released before `J_i` can finish is at or after `J_i` is certainly released.
Given a work-conserving scheduler, this means the processor will not be idle waiting for `J_i` if there are other jobs from `J_S` that are ready or become ready.
Therefore, there cannot be any idle interval between the execution of any two jobs within `J_S`.
key_insights: The emptiness of `J_delta` is a strong indicator of continuous processor utilization by `J_S`.

informal_sketch.intuition: If an external job `J_x` manages to sneak into an idle gap between jobs in `J_S`, it must be because there *was* an idle gap (`J_delta` was not empty), and `J_x` was ready (released) before that idle gap could potentially close.
steps: Assume `J_x` interferes by executing in an idle interval within `J_S`.
For such an idle interval to exist, `J_delta` cannot be empty (as per Lemma 3, if `J_delta` is empty, no idle intervals exist within `J_S`).
If `J_x` is to be scheduled in this idle interval, it must be ready (released) by the time the idle interval occurs.
The latest an idle interval could end is `delta_M(v_p)` (from Formula (delta_M(v_p))).
Therefore, `J_x` must be released before `delta_M(v_p)` for it to be considered for scheduling during such an idle period. Specifically, `r_min_x < delta_M(v_p)` ensures it *could* be ready.
Thus, both `J_delta != EMPTY_SET` and `r_min_x < delta_M(v_p)` must hold.

def check_lemma_4(J_x, J_S, J_P, all_jobs_J, v_p, scheduling_policy):
    if not scheduling_policy.is_work_conserving:
        return False

    J_delta = compute_J_delta(J_S, v_p) # Formula (2)
    delta_M_val = compute_delta_M(v_p, J_S) # Formula (delta_M(v_p))

    # The lemma states: IF J_x can interfere via idle interval THEN (J_delta is not empty AND J_x.r_min < delta_M_val)
    # So, we check the RHS. If it's true, interference is possible.
    # Note: The paper's formula (3) has J_delta = EMPTY_SET, which is a likely typo based on context and example.
    # We use J_delta != EMPTY_SET here.
    if J_delta and J_x.r_min < delta_M_val:
        return True # Condition for interference via idle interval is met
    return False

It links the existence of idle intervals (`J_delta`) with the release times of external jobs (`r_min_x`).

formal_description.conclusion: This recursive equation calculates an upper bound on the start time of a job J_i within a safe reduction set J_M.

informal_sketch.intuition: To find the latest a job `J_i` could possibly start, we consider the worst-case scenario: it's blocked by a lower-priority job, and then all higher-priority jobs that could possibly interfere (released before `J_i` starts) actually do. This is an iterative process because the set of interfering jobs depends on `J_i`'s potential start time.
steps: **1. Initial Blocking (s_i_0):** Calculate an initial upper bound for `J_i`'s start time. This considers:
a. The latest processor availability `A_max_1`.
b. The worst-case blocking from a lower-priority job in `J_M` (if any), which would execute for its `C_max` just before `J_i` is certainly released (`r_max_i - 1`).

**2. Iterative Interference (s_i_k):** In subsequent iterations, `s_i_k` is calculated by adding to the previous bound `s_i_k_minus_1` the worst-case execution time (`C_max_j`) of all *higher-priority* jobs `J_j` (from `J_M`) that could have been released in the interval `(s_i_k_minus_2, s_i_k_minus_1]`.
This process continues until `s_i_k` no longer increases (converges).
key_insights: This is a fixed-point iteration approach to find the worst-case start time.
It accounts for both blocking from lower-priority jobs and interference from higher-priority jobs.
Using `r_max_i` and `C_max_j` ensures a pessimistic (safe) upper bound.

Compare the current iteration's result (`s_i_k`) with the previous iteration's result (`s_i_k_minus_1`).
If they are equal, it means no new interfering jobs were found in the last interval, and the calculation has converged to its final value.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_convergence(s_i_k, s_i_k_minus_1):
    return s_i_k == s_i_k_minus_1
key_insights: Convergence ensures that the calculated upper bound is stable and comprehensive.
It's a standard termination condition for fixed-point iterations.

informal_sketch.intuition: The iterative process for `s_i(v_p)` adds the execution time of higher-priority jobs that are released within a growing time window. Since there's a finite number of such jobs, eventually all relevant ones will be included, and the process will stop.
steps: Each time `s_i_k` increases in Formula (6), it means that at least one new higher-priority job `J_j` (from `J_M`) was found to be released within the newly extended interval `(s_i_k_minus_2, s_i_k_minus_1]`.
Since there are only `|J_M(v_p)|` jobs in total within the reduction set, and `J_i` itself is one of them, there are at most `|J_M(v_p)| - 1` other jobs that could potentially interfere.
Therefore, the number of times `s_i_k` can strictly increase is limited by the number of distinct interfering jobs, which is at most `|J_M(v_p)| - 1`.
This guarantees that the iteration will converge in at most `|J_M(v_p)|` steps (including the initial step).

    # Each time s_i_k increases, it must be due to adding at least one of these jobs.
    # Thus, the number of increases is bounded by the number of such jobs.
key_insights: The finiteness of the job set guarantees convergence.
Each iteration effectively 'consumes' at least one new interfering job, leading to a clear upper bound on complexity.

informal_sketch.intuition: The calculation of `s_i(v_p)` (Formula (6)) is designed to be pessimistic, considering the worst-case blocking and interference. Therefore, `J_i` can never actually start later than this calculated `s_i(v_p)`.
steps: The proof is by contradiction: assume `J_i` starts later than `s_i(v_p)`.
This would imply either a larger blocking from a lower-priority job or larger interference from higher-priority jobs than accounted for in Formula (6).

**Case (i) - Larger Blocking:** Formula (6) already considers the maximum `C_max` of any lower-priority job in `J_M` and the latest processor availability `A_max_1`. Thus, no larger blocking is possible.

**Case (ii) - Larger Interference:** Formula (6) iteratively sums the `C_max` of all higher-priority jobs in `J_M` that could be released and interfere up to the calculated start time. If `J_i` starts later, it would mean more interference, but the iterative process of Formula (6) is designed to include all such interference up to its convergence point.
Since neither larger blocking nor larger interference is possible, the initial assumption must be false. Thus, `J_i` starts no later than `s_i(v_p)`.

assumptions: Non-preemptive work-conserving JLFP scheduling policy.
formal_description.conclusion: This provides sufficient conditions for a candidate set J_S to be a safe reduction set.

informal_sketch.intuition: A set of jobs `J_S` is 'safe to reduce' if no external job can interfere with it. This lemma provides two conditions to check for such interference: one for interference via idle periods (work-conserving property) and one for interference via higher priority (priority-driven property). If neither type of interference is possible, `J_S` is safe.
steps: **1. Check for Work-Conserving Interference:** Ensure that no job `J_x` (outside `J_S` and `J_P`) can execute in an idle interval within `J_S`. This is true if the condition `(J_delta != EMPTY_SET AND r_min_x < delta_M(v_p))` (from Lemma 4) does not hold for any `J_x`.

**2. Check for Priority-Driven Interference:** Ensure that no job `J_y` (from `J_high`) can start before a lower-priority job `J_l` in `J_S`. This is true if, for every `J_y` with higher priority than some `J_l` in `J_S`, `J_y`'s earliest release time (`r_min_y`) is *after* `J_l`'s latest possible start time (`LST_l(J_S, v_p)`).
If both conditions hold, then no job can interfere with `J_S`.
By Definition 6, if no job can interfere, `J_S` is a safe reduction set.
key_insights: This lemma provides the core logic for identifying safe reduction sets, enabling POR.
It systematically checks for all possible ways an external job could interfere, based on scheduler properties.
It relies on pessimistic bounds (`LST_l`, `r_min_y`) to ensure safety.

assumptions: Jobs in J_M are scheduled non-preemptively.
No other jobs (outside J_M) interfere with the execution of jobs in J_M.
formal_description.conclusion: This algorithm computes an upper bound on the latest time by which all jobs in J_M can complete their execution.

informal_sketch.intuition: To find the absolute latest time a group of jobs can finish, we assume the worst-case scenario: all jobs release as late as possible, execute for their maximum time, and are scheduled in an order that maximizes delay (latest release, then highest priority).
steps: **1. Order Jobs:** Sort the jobs in `J_M` primarily by their latest release time (`r_max`) in ascending order. If `r_max` values are tied, sort by highest priority (`p`). This ensures we consider jobs that become ready latest, potentially delaying subsequent jobs.
**2. Initialize Finish Time:** Start with `LF_T_val` as the latest time the processor is available (`A_max_1`) from the previous state `v_p`.
**3. Iterate and Accumulate:** For each job `J_k` in the sorted list:
a. The job `J_k` cannot start before it's certainly released (`J_k.r_max`) and the processor is certainly available (`LF_T_val`). So, its latest start time is `max(LF_T_val, J_k.r_max)`.
b. Add its worst-case execution time (`J_k.C_max`) to this start time to get its latest finish time. This becomes the new `LF_T_val` for the next job.
**4. Return:** The final `LF_T_val` is the latest finish time for all jobs in `J_M`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def compute_LFT(job_set_J_M, system_state_v_p):
    # 1. Sort jobs
    sorted_J_M = sorted(job_set_J_M, key=lambda job: (job.r_max, job.p)) # Assuming lower p is higher priority

    # 2. Initialize LF_T_val
    LF_T_val = system_state_v_p.A_max_1 # Latest processor available time from v_p

    # 3. Iterate and accumulate
    for J_k in sorted_J_M:
        latest_start_time = max(LF_T_val, J_k.r_max)
        LF_T_val = latest_start_time + J_k.C_max

    # 4. Return
    return LF_T_val
key_insights: This algorithm simulates a 'greedy' worst-case schedule.
Sorting by `r_max` and `p` ensures that jobs are considered in an order that maximizes delay.
Using `C_max` ensures the latest possible completion for each job.

The scheduling policy is work-conserving.

informal_sketch.intuition: Algorithm 3 calculates the latest possible finish time by assuming the most pessimistic conditions: jobs release as late as possible and execute for their maximum duration. Since these are the most delaying assumptions, no real scenario can possibly result in a later completion time.
steps: Algorithm 3 sorts jobs by latest release and highest priority, then sequentially adds their maximum execution times, respecting latest release times and processor availability.
This process inherently finds the maximum possible cumulative execution time and maximum possible idle time for the given set of jobs.
Any actual execution scenario will involve release times `r_i <= r_max_i` and execution times `C_i <= C_max_i`.
Therefore, the total workload and potential idle times in any real scenario will be less than or equal to what Algorithm 3 calculates, meaning the actual finish time cannot be later.
key_insights: The proof relies on the fact that `r_max` and `C_max` represent the absolute maximums.
The sequential accumulation in Algorithm 3 ensures that processor availability and release times are always respected, leading to a valid upper bound.

formal_description.statement: The LFT of a safe reduction set J_M is exact iff the set of jobs J_M cannot complete its execution later than LFT and there exists an execution scenario such that all jobs in J_M have completed exactly at LFT.

variables.LFT_val: A candidate value for the latest finish time
variables.J_M: A safe reduction set of jobs
variables.finish_time(J_M, gamma): The actual finish time of all jobs in J_M in scenario gamma

formal_description.conclusion: This defines what an 'exact latest finish time' means for a safe reduction set.

informal_sketch.intuition: An 'exact' latest finish time (LFT) is not just an upper bound, but the *tightest* possible upper bound. It means no scenario can finish later, and there's at least one specific scenario where the jobs finish at exactly that time.
steps: An `LFT_val` is exact for a safe reduction set `J_M` if two conditions are met:
**1. Upper Bound:** In *all* possible execution scenarios, the actual finish time of `J_M` must be less than or equal to `LFT_val`.
**2. Achievability:** There must exist at least one specific execution scenario where the jobs in `J_M` complete their execution at precisely `LFT_val`.
key_insights: Exactness combines the concepts of safety (upper bound) and tightness (achievability).
This is a stronger property than just being an 'upper bound'.

formal_description.statement: There exists an execution scenario such that all jobs in J_M have completed exactly at LF_T(J_M, v_p) as returned by line 5 of Algorithm 3.

variables.J_M: A safe reduction set of jobs
variables.LF_T_J_M_v_p: The latest finish time computed by Algorithm 3

assumptions: Each job J_i IN J_M releases at its latest possible time (r_max_i).
Each job J_i IN J_M executes for its worst-case execution time (C_max_i).
The processor becomes available at its latest possible time (A_max_1) after state v_p.
formal_description.conclusion: The LF_T(J_M, v_p) value computed by Algorithm 3 is achievable in at least one scenario.

informal_sketch.intuition: Algorithm 3 is designed to find the latest finish time by making the most pessimistic assumptions. If we actually create an execution scenario that matches these pessimistic assumptions, then the jobs will indeed finish at the time calculated by Algorithm 3.
steps: Construct a specific execution scenario `gamma_exact` where:
a. For every job `J_i` in `J_M`, its actual release time `r_i` is set to `J_i.r_max`.
b. For every job `J_i` in `J_M`, its actual execution time `C_i` is set to `J_i.C_max`.
c. The processor becomes available at `A_max_1` (the latest possible time from `v_p`).
When Algorithm 3 simulates this `gamma_exact` scenario, it will produce `LF_T(J_M, v_p)` as the finish time.
Therefore, such a scenario exists where `J_M` completes exactly at `LF_T(J_M, v_p)`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def demonstrate_LFT_achievability(job_set_J_M, system_state_v_p, computed_LFT):
    # Create the specific scenario
    gamma_exact = ExecutionScenario(job_set_J_M)
    for J_i in job_set_J_M:
        gamma_exact.release_times[J_i.id] = J_i.r_max
        gamma_exact.execution_times[J_i.id] = J_i.C_max

    # Simulate this scenario
    actual_finish_time = simulate_actual_finish_time(job_set_J_M, gamma_exact, system_state_v_p)

    return actual_finish_time == computed_LFT
key_insights: The algorithm's calculation directly corresponds to a concrete, pessimistic execution scenario.
This lemma is crucial for proving the 'tightness' aspect of the exact LFT.

formal_description.statement: The LF_T(J_M, v_p) as returned by line 5 of Algorithm 3 is the exact latest finish time of J_M.

variables.LF_T_J_M_v_p: The latest finish time computed by Algorithm 3 for J_M after state v_p
variables.J_M: A safe reduction set of jobs
variables.exact_LFT(J_M): The true exact latest finish time of J_M as per Definition 9

formal_description.conclusion: Algorithm 3 correctly computes the exact latest finish time for a safe reduction set.

informal_sketch.intuition: Since we've proven that Algorithm 3's result is both an upper bound (Lemma 8) and achievable (Lemma 9), it must be the *exact* latest finish time according to our definition of exact LFT (Definition 9).
steps: Recall Definition 9: an LFT is exact if it's an upper bound and it's achievable.
Lemma 8 establishes that `LF_T(J_M, v_p)` (from Algorithm 3) is indeed an upper bound on the finish time of `J_M`.
Lemma 9 establishes that `LF_T(J_M, v_p)` is achievable; there exists a scenario where `J_M` finishes at exactly that time.
Combining these two, `LF_T(J_M, v_p)` satisfies both conditions of Definition 9, thus it is the exact latest finish time.
key_insights: This corollary formally validates Algorithm 3's output for safe reduction sets.
It's a direct consequence of the preceding lemmas and definition.

results.identifier: Formula (5) - Sufficient Schedulability Test for J_M

formal_description.statement: FORALL J_i IN J_M, LF_T_i(J_M, v_p) <= d_i

variables.J_i: A job in the safe reduction set J_M
variables.J_M: The safe reduction set of jobs
variables.LF_T_i_J_M_v_p: An upper bound on the finish time of job J_i when scheduled after state v_p (calculated as s_i(v_p) + C_max_i)
variables.d_i: The absolute deadline of job J_i

formal_description.conclusion: This formula defines a sufficient schedulability test for the jobs within a safe reduction set J_M.

informal_sketch.intuition: To quickly check if a group of jobs (`J_M`) is schedulable, we calculate the latest possible finish time for each job within that group. If every job's latest finish time is still before its deadline, then we can be sure that no deadline will be missed by any job in `J_M`.
steps: For each job `J_i` in the safe reduction set `J_M`:
a. Calculate `s_i(v_p)`: an upper bound on `J_i`'s start time using Formula (6).
b. Calculate `LF_T_i(J_M, v_p)`: the upper bound on `J_i`'s finish time, which is `s_i(v_p) + J_i.C_max` (using its worst-case execution time).
c. Compare this `LF_T_i(J_M, v_p)` with `J_i`'s absolute deadline `d_i`.
If `LF_T_i(J_M, v_p) <= d_i` for *all* jobs `J_i` in `J_M`, then the entire set `J_M` is deemed schedulable.
key_insights: This is a 'sufficient' test: if it passes, it's definitely schedulable. If it fails, it *might* still be schedulable, but the test is too pessimistic to confirm.
It uses the pessimistic `s_i(v_p)` and `C_max_i` to ensure safety.
This test allows for early pruning of the state space if a reduction set is certainly schedulable.

formal_description.statement: A POR of a safe reduction set J_M as returned by line 8 of Algorithm 4 maintains safe response-time bounds.

variables.POR_of_J_M: The Partial-Order Reduction method applied to J_M
variables.J_M: A safe reduction set of jobs (identified by Algorithm 4)
variables.J_i: Any job (either in J_M or not in J_M)
variables.response_time(J_i, gamma): The actual response time of J_i in scenario gamma
variables.POR_of_J_M.BCRT(J_i): The best-case response time computed by the POR analysis for J_i
variables.POR_of_J_M.WCRT(J_i): The worst-case response time computed by the POR analysis for J_i

assumptions: J_M is a safe reduction set (as per Definition 6 and Lemma 5).
The POR of J_M does not affect the analysis of jobs not contained in J_M (Lemma 16, not provided).
The EFT and LFT for jobs in J_M are lower and upper bounds respectively (Lemma 15 and 13, mapped to Lemma 6 and Lemma 8).
formal_description.conclusion: The POR method provides safe (but not necessarily tight) response time bounds for all jobs in the system.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma confirms that applying Partial-Order Reduction (POR) to a 'safe reduction set' `J_M` won't break the safety of our response time calculations. While the bounds might not be perfectly tight, they will always correctly encompass the actual response times.
steps: **1. Jobs NOT in J_M:** For jobs `J_i` that are *not* part of the reduced set `J_M`, the POR technique is designed not to alter their analysis. Therefore, their response-time bounds remain as safe (and potentially exact) as in the original SAG analysis.
**2. Jobs IN J_M:** For jobs `J_i` that *are* part of the reduced set `J_M`:
a. The Earliest Finish Time (EFT) calculated for `J_M` (by Algorithm 2, proven exact by Corollary 1) serves as a lower bound for the completion of any job in `J_M`.
b. The Latest Finish Time (LFT) calculated for `J_M` (by Algorithm 3, proven exact by Corollary 2) serves as an upper bound for the completion of any job in `J_M`.
c. These exact EFT/LFT bounds for the *set* `J_M` can be used to derive safe (but not necessarily tight) individual BCRT/WCRT bounds for jobs *within* `J_M`.
Since all jobs (both inside and outside `J_M`) have safe response-time bounds, the overall POR maintains safe response-time bounds for the entire system (as per condition (i) of Definition 4).
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def verify_lemma_17(por_method, J_M, all_jobs_J):
    # Assume J_M is a safe reduction set from Algorithm 4

    # Part 1: Jobs not in J_M
    # (Relies on Lemma 16, which states POR doesn't affect other jobs' analysis)
    # If original analysis was safe, these remain safe.

    # Part 2: Jobs in J_M
    # EFT_JM = compute_EFT(J_M, v_p) # Corollary 1 proves this is exact EFT for the set
    # LFT_JM = compute_LFT(J_M, v_p) # Corollary 2 proves this is exact LFT for the set

    # These exact set-level bounds can be used to derive safe individual bounds.
    # For example, BCRT(J_i) for J_i in J_M could be EFT_JM - (sum of C_max of other jobs in J_M) - J_i.r_max
    # WCRT(J_i) for J_i in J_M could be LFT_JM - J_i.r_min
    # The key is that these derived bounds will be safe (contain the true RT).

    # Overall, the POR_method will satisfy condition (i) of Definition 4.
    return True
key_insights: The safety of POR for response times is guaranteed by the exactness of the EFT/LFT calculations for the reduced set.
It explicitly allows for some over-estimation (or under-estimation) of individual job response times within the reduced set, trading tightness for scalability.
This lemma is critical for satisfying Definition 5 (safe POR).
